paragraphs: Complex image prompts require a generator to coordinate objects, their details, and their positions. This paper introduces dense blob representations as an intermediate description of a scene. These visual primitives carry detailed information while remaining modular, interpretable to people, and straightforward to construct. They provide additional grounding for a text-to-image model beyond the prompt itself.

The authors build BlobGEN, a diffusion model that generates images using these representations. Its masked cross-attention module separates how different blob descriptions interact with visual features, supporting compositional control. They also introduce an in-context learning method that lets a large language model produce blob representations from text, connecting language-based scene planning to the image generator.

Experiments report better zero-shot generation quality and layout control on MS-COCO. With language-model assistance, the method also improves numerical and spatial correctness on compositional generation benchmarks. These findings support using an explicit scene representation to help a generator follow object counts and spatial arrangements, alongside producing visually strong images.
icml-2024-compositional-text-to-image-ge.tldr: BlobGEN uses interpretable scene primitives to improve text-to-image composition, layout control, and adherence to object counts and spatial relationships.

paragraphs: A stochastic block model generates a network by assigning nodes to communities and randomly creating connections with probabilities determined by community membership. Recovering those hidden groups is a central community-detection problem. This paper asks when exact recovery remains possible under edge differential privacy, where the privacy requirement concerns individual connections in the network.

The authors derive recovery conditions for three settings: communities of unequal sizes, a general structure that includes outliers, and a censored model with edge features. Their private algorithms run in polynomial time in the graph size. This broadens the analysis beyond the equal-sized communities covered by the previous best results described in the abstract.

As the privacy parameter epsilon tends to infinity, the algorithms' recovery thresholds match those of the non-private setting. This is a limiting statement as the privacy restriction relaxes, rather than a claim of identical thresholds at every privacy level. The contribution combines broader network models, efficient computation, and explicit conditions under which privacy and exact community recovery can coexist.
icml-2024-differentially-private-exact-r.tldr: The paper gives polynomial-time private community-recovery algorithms for three stochastic block models, with non-private thresholds recovered as epsilon grows without bound.

paragraphs: Learning a conditional distribution means learning how the range and likelihood of possible outcomes change with the input variables. A model therefore needs to represent many related distributions, rather than one overall distribution or one predicted outcome per input. This paper develops a neural entropic optimal transport approach for that task, with particular attention to limited-data settings.

The method trains two neural networks through a minimax objective. The generative network represents conditional inverse cumulative distribution functions, which describe outcomes by their probability levels. The other network represents a conditional Kantorovich potential used in the optimal transport formulation. Together, these components turn the conditional-distribution problem into a trainable generative procedure.

To discourage overfitting, the objective penalizes the Lipschitz constant of network outputs, constraining how sharply they can change. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate effectiveness relative to leading conditional-distribution learning techniques. The approach matters because it combines a distribution-generating representation with an explicit smoothness control, addressing both flexible conditional modeling and the difficulty of learning from small samples.
icml-2024-generative-conditional-distrib.tldr: Two jointly trained networks use entropic optimal transport and smoothness regularization to learn generative conditional distributions, particularly with limited data.

paragraphs: Generative Flow Networks generate combinatorial objects with desired properties. Their training involves maintaining flow balance, while traditional reinforcement learning commonly optimizes accumulated reward. This paper connects those perspectives through a training framework whose rewards depend on the policy. The connection makes it possible to derive policy-based training methods for GFlowNets.

The authors contrast these methods with existing GFlowNet approaches that resemble value-based reinforcement learning. They also address the backward policy, whose design affects training efficiency. Their coupled strategy learns the forward policy and designs the backward policy jointly, bringing two connected parts of the training problem into the same optimization process.

The paper supplies performance analysis and a theoretical guarantee for its policy-based framework. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets support using reinforcement-learning ideas for more robust gradient estimation and improved GFlowNet performance. The significance is both conceptual and practical: expressing flow balance through expected reward opens another route to training, while joint policy learning addresses an efficiency-sensitive design choice within that route.
icml-2024-gflownet-training-by-policy-gr.tldr: A policy-gradient framework connects GFlowNet flow balance to reward optimization and jointly trains forward and backward policies.

paragraphs: Self-attention allows information to move between positions in a sequence, but how training turns that flexibility into learned causal structure is less understood. The authors introduce an in-context learning task with a hidden causal graph. They use this controlled setting to analyze how gradient descent can teach a transformer the dependencies needed to solve the task.

For a simplified two-layer transformer, they prove that training encodes the latent causal graph in the first attention layer. The proof connects the attention-matrix gradient to mutual information between tokens. Through the data processing inequality, the largest gradient entries correspond to edges in the hidden graph, explaining how the learning signal identifies relevant connections.

When the input sequences come from in-context Markov chains, the analysis further shows that the transformer learns an induction head. Experiments on the proposed task demonstrate recovery of varied causal structures. These results provide a specific mechanism for causal-structure learning within the analyzed setup, connecting attention updates to statistical dependencies rather than asserting unrestricted causal discovery by transformers.
icml-2024-how-transformers-learn-causal-.tldr: On a designed in-context task, gradient descent teaches a simplified transformer to encode a hidden causal graph through attention gradients linked to mutual information.

paragraphs: Classical optimal-path problems seek a best path through a collection of possible choices. This paper replaces that hard selection with a probabilistic formulation. It represents a broad range of dynamic programming problems as directed acyclic graphs and assigns a Gibbs distribution over their paths, making path selection compatible with probabilistic inference.

The authors use properties of the Gumbel distribution to establish an equivalent message-passing algorithm. They then develop the components needed for variational Bayesian inference over an unobserved path, calling the resulting framework Bayesian dynamic programming. This connects the graph structure of a dynamic program with a distribution over possible latent solutions.

The proposed BDP-VAE places structured, sparse paths inside the latent space of a variational autoencoder. This allows end-to-end training for generative tasks that depend on structural information not directly observed in the data. The authors validate the approach's behavior and demonstrate applications in text-to-speech and singing voice synthesis, showing how probabilistic paths can function as learned internal structure in generative models.
icml-2024-latent-optimal-paths-by-gumbel.tldr: Gumbel-based message passing turns dynamic-programming paths into probabilistic latent variables for end-to-end generative modeling.

paragraphs: Multi-fidelity surrogate modeling combines sources with different levels of accuracy to predict the highest-fidelity result. Neural approaches improve scalability over traditional Gaussian-process methods, but often share only encoded representations across fidelity levels. The paper identifies this omission of decoder parameters as a weakness, particularly when high-fidelity training data covers only a limited part of the input domain.

Multi-fidelity Residual Neural Processes addresses the problem by combining outputs from lower-fidelity models and explicitly learning the residual between that combination and the highest-fidelity target. Because aggregation happens through decoded outputs, the decoders participate in information sharing. Lower-fidelity decoders are optimized to capture relationships both within their own fidelity and across fidelity levels.

The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on partial differential equation learning and a real-world climate modeling task. The architectural contribution is a concrete way to make lower-fidelity predictions useful to the final target: learn their combined contribution and then model its remaining error. This directly addresses the information-sharing weakness identified in earlier neural surrogate approaches.
icml-2024-multi-fidelity-residual-neural.tldr: MFRNP combines lower-fidelity model outputs and learns their residual error to improve high-fidelity surrogate predictions.

paragraphs: This paper develops iterative algorithms for finding dense subgraphs and computing dense subgraph decompositions. For the first problem, multiplicative weights update requires O(log(m)/epsilon²) iterations, while an area-convexity method requires O(log(m)/epsilon). Both have nearly linear work per iteration. The multiplicative-weights approach also simplifies recovering a subgraph from its fractional solution and avoids binary search.

The area-convexity algorithm improves an earlier iteration bound by a factor equal to the graph's maximum degree. Its total theoretical runtime matches the fastest flow-based bound cited in the abstract. For dense subgraph decomposition, the authors introduce an accelerated random coordinate descent algorithm with runtime O(mn log(1/epsilon)), giving logarithmic dependence on the requested precision.

That precision dependence is especially useful when a very accurate decomposition is needed. In the stated high-precision regime, epsilon much smaller than 1/n, the method can recover an exact solution in O(mn log n) total time, matching the cited exact flow-based algorithm. Experiments also show scalability to very large graphs and competitive performance against widely used methods with weaker guarantees.
icml-2024-multiplicative-weights-update-.tldr: New iterative dense-subgraph algorithms improve convergence guarantees while remaining practical on large graphs.

paragraphs: Diffusion models depend on score-function estimates during both training and generation. The paper identifies a tradeoff in commonly used estimators: learned neural approximations introduce bias, while Monte Carlo estimators based on the conditional score can have high variance. It proposes a nearest-neighbour estimator that uses multiple training examples to substantially reduce that variance.

The first application is training consistency models. With the proposed estimator, the authors report significantly faster convergence and better generated samples. This links the quality of the training signal to the quality and speed of model learning: reducing variability in score estimates improves outcomes in the consistency-model experiments described in the abstract.

The second application concerns probability-flow ordinary differential equation integration in diffusion models. The authors show that their estimator can take the place of a learned network for this computation. This demonstrates an additional use for training-data-based score estimation beyond supplying a learning target. The result opens a possible direction for diffusion sampling methods, without establishing that the replacement is preferable in every setting.
icml-2024-nearest-neighbour-score-estima.tldr: A nearest-neighbour score estimator reduces variance, improves consistency-model training, and can replace a learned network in diffusion probability-flow integration.

paragraphs: Code models are commonly trained on program text, which may leave gaps in their understanding of what happens when a program runs. NExT addresses that gap by teaching a language model to inspect execution traces: the variable states associated with executed lines. The aim is to connect explanations of program behavior with successful solutions to tasks such as code repair.

The method uses self-training to construct synthetic execution-aware reasoning examples. It bootstraps explanations that lead to correct task solutions, avoiding the need for extensive manual annotation. This makes runtime information part of the training process and gives the model examples that connect changing program states to a successful repair.

On repair tasks based on MBPP and HumanEval, NExT improves a PaLM 2 model's fix rate by 26.1 and 10.3 percentage points, respectively. Automated evaluation and human raters also find significantly better rationale quality. The trained model can generalize to situations without execution traces at test time, indicating that trace-based training can provide benefits even when those inputs are later unavailable.
icml-2024-next-teaching-large-language-m.tldr: NExT uses self-generated training examples grounded in execution traces to improve code repair and explanations of runtime behavior.

paragraphs: The Partial Credit Model describes integer-valued responses whose adjacent values represent meaningful progress, such as partial test scores or product ratings. This paper introduces a spectral algorithm for statistical inference under that model. Its goal is to combine accurate parameter estimation with substantially faster computation, making the model easier to use across different application settings.

The authors provide a non-asymptotic statistical analysis, so the guarantees address finite amounts of data. Under sampling assumptions, the algorithm achieves optimal error guarantees according to three different metrics. They also use its computational efficiency to develop an expectation-maximization algorithm for mixtures of Partial Credit Models, extending the approach to a richer modeling setting.

Experiments cover synthetic data and real applications in educational testing, recommendation, and financial investment. The spectral method is competitive with previous algorithms in accuracy while running orders of magnitude faster. Together, these findings connect a finite-sample theoretical guarantee with a practical speed advantage, and show how a faster inference component can support learning mixtures as well as individual models.
icml-2024-novel-spectral-algorithms-for-.tldr: A spectral Partial Credit Model estimator combines optimal finite-sample error guarantees under sampling assumptions with large empirical speed gains.

paragraphs: A mixture of experts combines several expert networks using weights supplied by a softmax gate. Although this architecture is widely used, analyzing how reliably its components can be estimated is difficult. This paper studies least-squares estimation for a deterministic mixture-of-experts regression model, moving beyond earlier theory centered on data generated by Gaussian mixture-of-experts models.

The analysis introduces a condition called strong identifiability to characterize estimation convergence for different expert functions. The central comparison concerns feed-forward experts using sigmoid or tanh activations and experts defined by polynomials. The authors show substantially faster estimation rates for the strongly identifiable neural-network experts, while polynomial experts can have surprisingly slow rates.

The result makes expert selection a statistical question as well as an architectural one. Different function choices can change how quickly estimation improves as more data becomes available, even within the same softmax-gated design. The paper's conclusions concern the analyzed regression setting and identifiability condition, providing theoretical guidance about which expert families support more favorable least-squares estimation behavior.
icml-2024-on-least-square-estimation-in-.tldr: Strong identifiability explains why least-squares estimation can converge much faster for sigmoid and tanh experts than for polynomial experts.

paragraphs: Layer normalization is widely used, but its contribution to what a network can represent remains incompletely understood. This paper studies it as a source of nonlinearity. The authors analyze an LN-Net, a network constructed by repeatedly composing linear transformations with layer normalization, to isolate the expressive capacity of that combination.

They prove that an LN-Net with just three neurons per layer and O(m) normalization layers can correctly classify m samples with any assignment of labels. They also establish a lower bound on its VC dimension. These results show substantial capacity in a narrow network when sufficient depth is available; the classification theorem concerns representing the supplied sample labels.

The paper further shows, under a mild assumption, that dividing features into groups can amplify layer normalization's nonlinearity. Experiments support this effect and the effectiveness of architectures designed to exploit it. The contribution therefore connects a theoretical account of normalization's expressive power to a concrete architectural direction: using and strengthening that nonlinearity when designing neural networks.
icml-2024-on-the-nonlinearity-of-layer-n.tldr: Layer normalization supplies substantial representational nonlinearity, and grouping can amplify it under the paper's stated assumption.

paragraphs: Offline decision-making uses previously collected data to choose actions. With function approximation, the learner must work within a chosen class of value or prediction functions while relying on whatever information the data contains. This paper characterizes statistical limits for this setting in stochastic contextual bandits and Markov decision processes.

The authors establish optimal or nearly optimal minimax rates. Their characterization combines the pseudo-dimension of the function class with a new description of the behavior policy that generated the data. Pseudo-dimension captures function-class complexity, while the behavior-policy characterization addresses data coverage. The latter strictly generalizes the previous coverage notions identified in the abstract, bringing them within a broader account of what makes offline data informative.

The paper also studies how offline data can help when a learner subsequently makes decisions online. It obtains nearly minimax-optimal rates across a wide range of regimes. Together, the results address both learning from a fixed dataset and using that dataset to support further interaction, relating attainable performance to model complexity and the data-generating policy.
icml-2024-on-the-statistical-complexity-.tldr: The paper characterizes near-optimal offline decision-making rates through function-class complexity and a broader notion of behavior-policy coverage.

paragraphs: Answering complex questions about a data stream with a large language model can make inference prohibitively expensive. This paper proposes learning a cascade that begins with smaller models and ends with an LLM. A deferral policy decides which model should handle each input, making model selection part of the system's learned behavior.

The authors formulate online cascade learning as imitation learning. Smaller models are updated over time using collected demonstrations from the LLM, allowing the cascade to learn while processing the stream. They provide a no-regret algorithm for this formulation. The approach therefore combines ongoing training with routing, rather than treating the cheaper models as a fixed set of alternatives.

Across four benchmarks, the method achieves accuracy comparable to the LLM while reducing inference costs by as much as 90%. The experiments also report strong robustness to shifts in the input distribution. These are empirical results for the evaluated settings, supporting the usefulness of continuously learned cascades when a stream must be processed economically without sacrificing much predictive accuracy.
icml-2024-online-cascade-learning-for-ef.tldr: Online cascades learn smaller models from LLM demonstrations and route inputs to cut inference costs while maintaining comparable benchmark accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies two transformer weaknesses: sensitivity to corrupted inputs and rank collapse in output representations. Its analysis interprets self-attention as an autonomous state-space model. In that view, attention promotes smoothness, which can produce lower-rank outputs and reduce representational capacity. The model's steady-state solution is also sensitive to perturbations of its input.

The authors introduce proportional-integral-derivative feedback control with a reference point into this state-space formulation. The control mechanism aims to preserve high-frequency details and improve stability. They prove robustness and an ability to address rank collapse for the resulting controlled model, providing a theoretical motivation for changing the attention-based architecture.

This framework leads to PIDformer, a class of PID-controlled transformers intended to improve noise resilience and retain richer representations. The paper evaluates the models against baseline transformers on object classification, image segmentation, and language modeling. Its contribution connects an analysis of attention dynamics to a control-based architectural intervention, with theoretical results for the controlled formulation and empirical evaluation across several practical tasks.
icml-2024-pidformer-transformer-meets-co.tldr: PIDformer introduces feedback control into an attention-inspired state-space model to address input sensitivity and representation rank collapse.

paragraphs: Estimating information-theoretic quantities becomes difficult as data dimensionality grows. REMEDI targets differential entropy, a central quantity for continuous distributions. Its approach combines fitting a simple adaptive base model with estimating how that model differs from the data distribution, using the discrepancy to improve the entropy estimate.

The method minimizes the base model's cross-entropy and estimates its relative-entropy deviation from the data density. This separates the task into a tractable modeling component and a correction for remaining mismatch. The authors also extend theoretical consistency results to the more general setting required by their method, supporting the framework beyond its experimental performance.

Experiments show improved entropy estimation across synthetic and natural data. The paper further adapts the framework to information-theoretic supervised learning, focusing on the Information Bottleneck approach, where it reports better accuracy than existing methods. It also explores connections to generative modeling through rejection sampling and Langevin dynamics. These contributions position corrective density estimation as useful both for measuring information and for incorporating information-based objectives into learning.
icml-2024-remedi-corrective-transformati.tldr: REMEDI improves entropy estimation by fitting a simple base model and estimating a correction for its mismatch with the data distribution.

paragraphs: This paper theoretically compares reinforcement learning from human feedback and direct preference optimization. The analysis focuses on loglinear policies and linear reward functions, providing a defined setting in which to compare the two approaches. It first assumes access to an oracle that exactly solves the relevant optimization problems.

Under that assumption, the authors derive minimax statistical bounds on each method's suboptimality gap. Their comparison jointly considers sample size, policy and reward dimensions, and regularization temperature. They then examine approximate optimization and establish exponentially decaying convergence rates for both approaches, separating statistical considerations from the effect of incomplete optimization.

The analysis also considers a true reward that cannot be represented by the assumed reward class. In this setting, RLHF incurs an additional constant error, while DPO retains an asymptotically decreasing gap with appropriate temperature tuning. The authors extend their exact-optimization comparison to Markov decision processes as well. These findings explain how the relative merits depend on modeling choices and optimization conditions, rather than establishing an unconditional winner.
icml-2024-reward-model-learning-vs-direc.tldr: Within specified policy and reward classes, the paper compares RLHF and DPO across statistical error, optimization, and reward misspecification.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning separates exploration from the eventual choice of reward function, so one exploration phase can support multiple objectives. This paper extends that idea to risk-sensitive learning using Conditional Value-at-Risk. The aim is to collect information once and then address CVaR-based decision-making for any given reward function within the proposed framework.

The authors introduce CVaR-RF-UCRL and prove an accuracy-and-confidence guarantee with a sample-complexity upper bound. They also establish a lower bound for any exploration algorithm in this framework. The bounds support a near-optimality claim while retaining different dependencies on the horizon and risk-tolerance parameter; the upper and lower bounds are not identical.

For the planning stage, the paper supplies CVaR-VI and a more practical variant, CVaR-VI-DISC. Numerical experiments support the approach's effectiveness and practicality. The overall contribution brings risk sensitivity into reusable exploration: the learner gathers data before a reward is specified, then uses dedicated planning procedures to address a risk-sensitive objective once the reward becomes available.
icml-2024-risk-sensitive-reward-free-rei.tldr: A CVaR-based framework enables one reward-free exploration phase to support later risk-sensitive planning, with sample-complexity guarantees.

paragraphs: Designing RNA requires accounting for both its sequence and its flexible three-dimensional conformations. RNAFlow addresses protein-conditioned RNA sequence and structure generation using flow matching. The paper highlights two challenges behind this design: RNA can adopt varied conformations, and fine-tuning a large structure-prediction network can be computationally costly.

RNAFlow's denoising network combines an RNA inverse-folding model with a pretrained RosettaFold2NA network. Inverse folding contributes sequence generation within the structure-denoising process. This integration allows the structure-prediction network to remain fixed during training, simplifying the learning problem while retaining that network as part of sequence-and-structure generation.

To better represent RNA's dynamic conformations, the authors further condition the inverse-folding model on inferred conformational ensembles. This supplies information about multiple conformations within the design process. Evaluations on protein-conditioned RNA sequence and structure generation show advantages over existing RNA design methods. The contribution brings flexible-structure modeling and a fixed pretrained predictor together in a joint design framework, addressing both conformational variability and the stated training-cost challenge.
icml-2024-rnaflow-rna-structure-sequence.tldr: RNAFlow combines inverse folding, flow matching, and a fixed structure predictor to generate protein-conditioned RNA sequences and structures.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a large language model under limited memory and compute requires choosing which changes to learn. RoSA keeps pretrained weights fixed and jointly trains two additions: a low-rank component and a highly sparse component. Inspired by robust principal component analysis, this combination aims to approximate the performance of full fine-tuning with a smaller trainable parameter budget.

The authors evaluate RoSA on challenging generative tasks, including grade-school mathematics and SQL generation. At the same parameter budget, it outperforms LoRA, purely sparse fine-tuning, and other hybrid methods. On some tasks it recovers full-fine-tuning performance, showing that the combined representation can close that performance gap in the evaluated cases.

The paper also supplies sparse GPU kernels to make the training method efficient in memory and computation. RoSA is compatible with low-precision pretrained weights, combining quantization with low-rank and sparse approximations. This systems support matters because the proposal includes both a way to allocate trainable parameters and an implementation designed to make that allocation computationally useful.
icml-2024-rosa-accurate-parameter-effici.tldr: RoSA combines low-rank and sparse updates to improve parameter-efficient fine-tuning, matching full fine-tuning on some evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Sliced Wasserstein methods compare distributions through projections, making the choice of projection directions important for applications that minimize this distance. Earlier direction-selection approaches can require expensive optimization or sampling. This paper proposes a slicing distribution that avoids optimization and supports fast sampling for Monte Carlo estimation.

Its basic construction draws one random vector from each input distribution, takes their difference, and normalizes it to obtain a random-path projecting direction. From this construction, the authors define a random-path slicing distribution and two distance variants: Random-Path Projection Sliced Wasserstein and an importance-weighted version. The projection mechanism therefore depends directly on samples from the distributions being compared.

The paper examines the variants' topological, statistical, and computational properties, and demonstrates favorable performance in gradient-flow applications and training image denoising diffusion models. The contribution addresses the cost of choosing useful projections as part of distribution comparison. It provides a sample-based direction construction together with theoretical analysis and applications, without requiring a separate optimization procedure to select the slicing distribution.
icml-2024-sliced-wasserstein-with-random.tldr: Random-path projections use normalized differences between distribution samples to select sliced Wasserstein directions without optimization.

paragraphs: A molecule's two-dimensional graph describes atoms and bonds, while a conformer describes one three-dimensional arrangement of its atoms. Multiple conformers can therefore contribute geometric information beyond the bond graph. This paper develops a molecular property predictor that combines the graph with several conformers, addressing approaches that process these representations in isolation.

The central aggregation mechanism uses a differentiable solver for the Fused Gromov-Wasserstein Barycenter problem. It integrates information from the two-dimensional structure and the collection of three-dimensional conformers. The method also uses distance geometry for efficient conformer generation and includes a GPU implementation of the aggregation procedure.

The authors prove that the aggregation is E(3)-invariant, so changing the geometric coordinate frame through Euclidean transformations does not change the aggregate representation. Experiments on established datasets show that the mechanism helps the proposed method significantly outperform state-of-the-art molecular property predictors. The contribution combines several geometric views of a molecule with its bond structure while preserving an appropriate invariance and supporting efficient computation.
icml-2024-structure-aware-e-3-invariant-.tldr: A differentiable, E(3)-invariant aggregation mechanism combines molecular graphs with multiple conformers to improve property prediction.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation helps a trained model handle shifted inputs, but many methods require backpropagation and editable weights. Those requirements can conflict with resource-limited deployments using quantized or hard-coded models. Forward-Optimization Adaptation addresses this setting by adapting through forward passes while leaving the model's weights unchanged.

FOA learns a newly added input prompt using a derivative-free covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy. To support online learning without labels, it evaluates candidates through a fitness function combining differences between test and training statistics with prediction entropy. An additional activation-shifting mechanism adjusts internal activations toward the source training domain for shifted test inputs.

On ImageNet-C, FOA applied to an 8-bit quantized vision transformer outperforms gradient-based TENT applied to a full-precision 32-bit vision transformer, with memory reductions reaching 24-fold. This comparison shows that the proposed adaptation mechanisms can be effective under a constrained deployment configuration. The result supports forward-only adaptation as a practical option when updating model weights through gradients is unavailable or costly.
icml-2024-test-time-model-adaptation-wit.tldr: FOA adapts frozen models using derivative-free prompt optimization and activation shifts, achieving strong ImageNet-C results with much lower memory use.

paragraphs: A model can have low average prediction error while occasionally producing outputs that violate important constraints. One practical response is to modify predictions at inference time so that they satisfy those constraints, avoiding retraining. This paper asks how that intervention affects generalization in multiclass classification, focusing on the role of the loss function.

The authors identify a class of losses for which imposing constraints preserves relative generalization error. Here, relative error means the gap compared with the best model, and the result says that this gap does not increase after the constraints are imposed. Softmax cross-entropy is among the popular losses with this property.

The paper also shows that some loss functions fail to preserve relative error under inference-time constraints. Consequently, the result depends on the loss and concerns a comparative error gap, rather than guaranteeing that every constrained prediction improves. The analysis gives a specific reason to consider loss selection when designing systems that enforce output rules after training: it can determine whether the stated generalization protection applies.
icml-2024-understanding-the-impact-of-in.tldr: For certain multiclass losses, including softmax cross-entropy, inference-time constraints do not increase the generalization-error gap relative to the best model.
